country.name: California
country.summary: California makes most of the wine the United States drinks, and the exam treats it as the reference state of the New World. The vines sit where the cold Pacific can reach them: the North Coast above San Francisco Bay, the Central Coast below it, with the hot Central Valley, the Sierra Foothills and Lodi inland and the South Coast below Los Angeles. There is no quality ladder. An American Viticultural Area is a line on a map that promises origin and nothing else, and the figures that matter are the percentages: 85 for an AVA, 75 for a variety or a county, 95 for a vintage on an AVA wine, and 100 per cent Californian fruit under state law whenever the word California is the appellation. Cabernet Sauvignon rules Napa, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay follow the fog, Zinfandel is the inherited grape, and the Judgment of Paris in 1976 is the founding story.
country.overview:
The Franciscan missions, founded from San Diego in 1769 to the last at Sonoma in 1823, carried the Mission grape up the coast. The Gold Rush of 1849 brought the drinkers and the money: Buena Vista at Sonoma in 1857, Charles Krug at St Helena in 1861, Schramsberg in 1862, Beringer in 1876 and Inglenook in 1879. Phylloxera then took the vineyards and Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, took the wineries. The modern industry was rebuilt after the Second World War on the research of the University of California at Davis, and on the Robert Mondavi Winery of 1966, the first large winery built in Napa since Prohibition. On 24 May 1976 a Paris tasting judged blind put a 1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon above the Bordeaux first growths and a 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay above the white Burgundies. The 1980s added the Bordeaux partnerships Opus One and Dominus, the Rhône Rangers of the Central Coast, and a second phylloxera: the AXR1 rootstock failed, and Napa and Sonoma were replanted through the 1990s.

The geography is one rule repeated. The California Current chills the ocean, the hot interior rises, and marine air is pulled inland through every gap in the Coast Ranges: through the Golden Gate into San Pablo Bay and the south of Napa, through the Petaluma Gap and the Russian River's mouth into Sonoma, down the Salinas Valley from Monterey Bay, through the Templeton Gap into Paso Robles, and straight up Santa Barbara's valleys, where the mountains run across the coast. Distance from a gap matters more than latitude. Inland, the Central Valley is hot, flat and irrigated and grows the everyday wine; Lodi at its northern end is cooled by the Delta and keeps old Zinfandel; the Sierra Foothills carry Gold Rush Zinfandel on granite in Amador and El Dorado.

The law is federal and thin. The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau approves AVAs on evidence of name, boundary and distinguishing climate, soil or elevation; Augusta in Missouri was the first in 1980 and Napa Valley the first in California in 1981. AVAs nest, and nothing in one fixes a grape, a yield, a method or a style. The label rules are percentages: variety 75, AVA 85, county 75, vintage 95 on an AVA wine and 85 otherwise; Estate Bottled needs fruit the winery owns or controls in its own AVA, made on its premises. California adds 100 per cent Californian grapes for any California appellation, and conjunctive labelling, so that a sub-AVA of Napa Valley prints Napa Valley beside it, a Sonoma AVA prints Sonoma County on wine bottled from 1 January 2014, and a Paso Robles district prints Paso Robles. Reserve, Old Vine and Barrel Select are unregulated words.

The exam leans on Napa's map, Sonoma's fog, the Judgment of Paris, Zinfandel as Primitivo, the percentages, and the houses every list carries.
ladder: A smaller AVA lying wholly inside a larger one: Oakville inside Napa Valley inside North Coast. The label may use any level it qualifies for at 85 per cent, and California's conjunctive labelling laws make the parent's name ride beside the child's for Napa Valley, Sonoma County and Paso Robles, the three the exam asks.

An American Viticultural Area approved by the federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau on evidence of name, boundary and distinguishing growing conditions: 85 per cent of the grapes must come from inside the line. It fixes origin only, never grape, yield, method or quality.

A political appellation such as Sonoma County or Santa Barbara County: 75 per cent of the grapes from the county under federal law. Up to three neighbouring counties may be named with their percentages, and the fruit must be entirely from those counties.
Federal law asks 75 per cent from the state, but California's own regulation requires 100 per cent Californian grapes for any wine that names California or any place within it as its appellation.

The country appellation, used when the grapes come from more than one state; since a federal rule of November 2012 it may carry a vintage when 85 per cent of the wine is from that year, and it is the bottom of the ladder and the origin of much bulk wine.
labels: Varietal
A single grape named on the label must be at least 75 per cent of the wine under federal law; the balance may be anything.
Vintage
95 per cent from the stated year when the appellation is an AVA; 85 per cent when it is a state or a county, and since November 2012 when it is American, which before then could carry no vintage.
Estate Bottled
100 per cent of the grapes from vineyards the winery owns or controls, inside the same AVA as the winery, crushed, finished and bottled on its own premises in one continuous process.
Produced and Bottled by
The named winery fermented at least 75 per cent of the wine; Made by means the same. Cellared by, Vinted by or Prepared by means only that it was treated and bottled there.
Reserve
No legal meaning in the United States, unlike Reserva in Spain or Riserva in Italy; the same is true of Old Vine, Barrel Select, Proprietor's and Private Reserve.
Meritage
A trademark licensed by an alliance of wineries for a Bordeaux-style blend of at least two Bordeaux grapes with none above 90 per cent; it rhymes with heritage.
Conjunctive labelling

California law makes a label that names a sub-AVA of Napa Valley also print Napa Valley, a Sonoma County AVA print Sonoma County on wine bottled from 1 January 2014, and a district of Paso Robles print Paso Robles.
Fumé Blanc
A name coined at the Robert Mondavi Winery in 1968 for dry, often barrel-aged Sauvignon Blanc; it is the same grape and the word carries no rule.
Table Wine
The federal term for a still wine of 7 to 14 per cent alcohol, which need not print its exact strength; above 14 per cent the figure must appear, with a tolerance of one point.
Contains Sulphites
Required on every wine of 10 parts per million or more, which is nearly all of them; it says nothing about how the wine was made.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The state's prestige red: ripe cassis, cedar and new French oak from Napa's benches and mountains, structured and age-worthy from the Santa Cruz Mountains, rounder from Alexander Valley and Paso Robles.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The most planted white grape: barrel-fermented, buttery and full from the warm valleys, tighter and citrus-led from Carneros, the Russian River Valley, Sta. Rita Hills and the Santa Cruz Mountains, and the base of traditional-method sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Lives in the fog: Carneros, the Russian River Valley, the Sonoma Coast, Anderson Valley, the Santa Lucia Highlands and Santa Barbara's Sta. Rita Hills and Santa Maria Valley, from silky and red-fruited to dark and plush.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: California's inherited grape, the same vine as Italy's Primitivo and Croatia's Tribidrag: brambly, peppery, high in alcohol from old head-trained vines in Dry Creek, Sonoma Valley, Lodi, Amador and Paso Robles; White Zinfandel is its off-dry pink.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Napa's second red and the softening half of its Bordeaux blends, a plush varietal from Three Palms and Carneros, and widely planted in the Central Valley for everyday wine.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Dry and often oaked as Fumé Blanc in Napa, grassy and crisp from Dry Creek, Lake County and Happy Canyon in Santa Barbara; the base of the state's rare botrytised sweet wines with Sémillon.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The Rhône Rangers' grape: peppery and cool from the Petaluma Gap, the Sonoma Coast and Santa Barbara, dense and warm from Paso Robles, usually labelled Syrah.

grapes.name: Petite Sirah
grapes.styles: Durif, the inky, tannic child of Syrah and Peloursin, an old field-blend partner of Zinfandel in Sonoma and Lodi and a dark varietal in its own right.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: Rhône-style blends and old vines in Paso Robles, the Sierra Foothills and Contra Costa; the G of the state's GSM blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A perfumed partner in Napa's proprietary reds, Dominus and the Oakville cult wines among them, and rarely bottled alone.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A small, dark seasoning in Meritage and proprietary blends, ripening fully in Napa's warmth.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Once the Central Valley's workhorse white for off-dry jug wine, now a small revival of dry old-vine bottlings from Clarksburg and Chalone.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot-scented white of the Rhône Rangers in Paso Robles, Santa Barbara and the Sierra Foothills, sometimes co-fermented with Syrah.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A cool-site white in Monterey's Arroyo Seco, Anderson Valley and Santa Barbara, and a partner in late-harvest botrytised wines.

exam: Hold the percentages in one breath: 75 for a variety, 85 for an AVA, 75 for a county, 95 for a vintage on an AVA wine, and 100 per cent Californian fruit under state law.
Say what an AVA is and is not: a federally approved boundary proving origin, with no rule on grape, yield, method or quality, nested one inside another.
Place the North Coast, the Central Coast, the Central Valley, Lodi, the Sierra Foothills and the South Coast on the map and give each its one wine.
Tell the Judgment of Paris story straight: 24 May 1976, the 1973 Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon and the 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay.
Know Zinfandel as Primitivo and Tribidrag, where the old vines are, and that White Zinfandel is an off-dry rosé that kept them in the ground.
Explain conjunctive labelling for Napa Valley, Sonoma County and Paso Robles, and why Reserve, Old Vine and Barrel Select mean nothing in law.
Name the Bordeaux partnerships, Opus One in Oakville and Dominus in Yountville, and the Rhône Rangers of the Central Coast.
traps: An AVA guarantees geography only; it is never a quality tier and never carries a grape or yield rule, unlike an AOP or a DOCG.
The varietal minimum is 75 per cent federally, so a Cabernet Sauvignon may legally carry a quarter of something else; Oregon's 90 per cent is Oregon's rule, not California's.
Chateau Montelena won Paris with Chardonnay and Stag's Leap Wine Cellars with Cabernet Sauvignon; reversing them is the classic error.
Sonoma County is a county appellation at 75 per cent; Sonoma Coast, Sonoma Valley and Northern Sonoma are AVAs at 85 per cent.
Petite Sirah is Durif, a cross of Syrah and Peloursin, not a small Syrah and not Syrah at all.
Zinfandel is not an American native grape: it is Primitivo, and its home is the Dalmatian coast of Croatia; it reached the east coast of the United States in the 1820s, before the Gold Rush.
Meritage is a trademark, not a legal category, and it rhymes with heritage, not with a French word.
The Central Valley and the Central Coast are different places: the valley is the hot interior of everyday wine, the coast is the Pacific strip of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Rhône grapes.

cards.f: US label percentages: variety, AVA, county, vintage
cards.b: Variety 75 per cent; AVA 85 per cent; county or state 75 per cent; vintage 95 per cent on an AVA wine, 85 on a state or county wine. California adds 100 per cent Californian fruit for a California appellation.

cards.f: What an AVA guarantees
cards.b: Origin only: a federally approved boundary with distinguishing name, climate, soil or elevation. No grape, yield, method, style or quality rule. AVAs nest; the first was Augusta, Missouri, 1980; Napa Valley was California's first, 1981.

cards.f: Judgment of Paris: date and two winners
cards.b: 24 May 1976, Paris, judged blind by French tasters. Red: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon. White: Chateau Montelena 1973 Chardonnay. Both houses are in Napa Valley.

cards.f: Zinfandel: its identity in Italy and Croatia
cards.b: One vine: Primitivo in Puglia and Tribidrag, also called Crljenak Kaštelanski, on Croatia's Dalmatian coast, its home. It reached the east coast of the United States in the 1820s, before the Gold Rush.

cards.f: Estate Bottled: what the term requires
cards.b: The winery sits in the labelled AVA, grew all the grapes on land it owns or controls inside that AVA, and crushed, fermented, finished, aged and bottled the wine on its premises in one continuous process.

cards.f: Conjunctive labelling: the three parents the exam asks
cards.b: Napa Valley beside any Napa sub-AVA (state law of 1990); Sonoma County beside any AVA wholly in the county, on wine bottled from 1 January 2014; Paso Robles beside any Paso district, on wine bottled from 1 January 2008.

cards.f: Meritage: meaning and rule
cards.b: A trademark for a Bordeaux-style blend licensed by an alliance of wineries: at least two Bordeaux grapes, none above 90 per cent. Not a legal category. Rhymes with heritage.

cards.f: Words with no legal meaning on a US label
cards.b: Reserve, Private Reserve, Special Selection, Old Vine, Barrel Select and Proprietor's Blend: none is defined in US law, unlike Reserva in Spain or Riserva in Italy, so each means only what the winery intends.

cards.f: California's six broad wine areas
cards.b: North Coast (Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino, Lake); Central Coast (Santa Cruz to Santa Barbara); Central Valley (bulk wine); Lodi (old Zinfandel by the Delta); Sierra Foothills (Amador, El Dorado Zinfandel); South Coast (Temecula).

cards.f: Petite Sirah: identity
cards.b: Durif, a French cross of Syrah and Peloursin: inky, tannic, peppery. Not a small Syrah. An old field-blend partner of Zinfandel in Sonoma, Lodi and the Central Valley.

questions.q: What minimum share of a wine must come from a named American Viticultural Area for the AVA to appear on the label?
questions.exp: Federal law sets 85 per cent for an AVA, 75 for a county or state and 75 for a named variety; California's own regulation raises the state figure to 100 per cent Californian grapes.

questions.q: Which Chardonnay won the white flight of the 1976 Paris tasting?
questions.exp: The Calistoga house's 1973 Chardonnay placed first among the whites; Chalone, Spring Mountain and Freemark Abbey were also Californian entrants in the same flight.

questions.q: Under which Italian name is Zinfandel grown in Puglia?
questions.exp: Zinfandel and Primitivo are one vine, traced to the Croatian grape Tribidrag; Negroamaro is Puglia's other red, Aglianico is Campania's and Nero d'Avola is Sicily's.

questions.q: What share of the grapes must be Californian when a wine names California as its appellation of origin?
questions.exp: California's own regulation demands that every grape be Californian when the state or any place within it is the appellation, stricter than the federal floor of 75 per cent for a state or county and 85 per cent for an AVA.

questions.q: Which was the first American Viticultural Area approved in California?
questions.exp: Napa Valley was approved in 1981, a year after Augusta in Missouri became the nation's first AVA; Santa Maria Valley, Santa Cruz Mountains and Sonoma Valley followed within months.

questions.q: What minimum share of a named grape variety must a Californian varietal wine contain under federal law?
questions.exp: The federal varietal minimum is 75 per cent, so a quarter of the blend may go unnamed; Oregon's 90 per cent is a state rule that does not apply in California.

questions.q: Which grape is Petite Sirah genetically?
questions.exp: Petite Sirah is Durif, a cross of Syrah and Peloursin found in a French nursery in the 1880s; it is neither of its parents, and Mourvèdre, the Mataro of old Californian field blends, is unrelated.

questions.q: Which Central Valley AVA, cooled by breezes off the Delta, is best known for old-vine Zinfandel?
questions.exp: Lodi, at the northern end of the Central Valley, keeps many of the state's oldest head-trained Zinfandel vines; Clarksburg is the Delta's Chenin Blanc district, and Madera and Dunnigan Hills are warmer valley AVAs.

regions.name: Napa & Sonoma (CA)
regions.summary: Napa and Sonoma are neighbouring counties north of San Francisco Bay, parted by the Mayacamas Mountains: one course heading, two appellations. Napa is a narrow valley of Cabernet Sauvignon, cool at Carneros by the bay and hot at Calistoga, with nested AVAs on floor, bench and mountain. Sonoma is wider and more varied: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in the fog of the Russian River Valley and the Sonoma Coast, Zinfandel in Dry Creek, rounder Cabernet in Alexander Valley. Napa won the 1976 Judgment of Paris, and a sub-AVA label must name its parent.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean, dry summers and winter rain, governed by fog. Cold air enters Napa from San Pablo Bay and thins northward, so Carneros is coolest and Calistoga, 50 kilometres up, hottest. Sonoma's fog comes through the Petaluma Gap and up the Russian River from Jenner; Alexander and Knights valleys lie inland and warm. Spring frost and autumn wildfire smoke are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Napa's variety is famous: volcanic ash and tuff on the Vaca side and the mountains, gravelly alluvial fans on the Oakville and Rutherford benches, clay by the river, clay loam in Carneros. Sonoma answers with Goldridge, a fine sandy loam of marine sediment under the Russian River Valley, volcanic ash on Chalk Hill, and gravel in Dry Creek and Alexander valleys.
terroir.topography: Napa is a trench about 50 kilometres (thirty miles) long and two to eight kilometres wide, running north-west from the bay to Calistoga, the Mayacamas on the west with Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain and Diamond Mountain, the Vaca Range on the east with Howell Mountain and Atlas Peak. Sonoma holds valleys between parallel ridges: Sonoma Valley, the Russian River plain, Dry Creek and Alexander valleys, and the coastal ridges above the fog.
terroir.water: The Napa River runs south into San Pablo Bay, the valley's cooling source. The Russian River rises in Mendocino, passes Healdsburg and reaches the Pacific at Jenner, the gap that admits Sonoma's fog. Lake Sonoma heads Dry Creek.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Napa's first grape by a distance: cassis, cedar, dusty tannin and new French oak from the benches, denser and grippier from the mountains; rounder and more supple in Sonoma's Alexander and Knights valleys.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Carneros, the Russian River Valley and Chalk Hill make the serious wine, barrel-fermented with lees and some malolactic; Sonoma Coast and the mountains give the tightest versions, and Napa's floor the fullest.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Sonoma's prize grape in the fog belt: silky, red-fruited and spiced in the Russian River Valley, darker and more saline on the Sonoma Coast, lighter in Carneros, where it also feeds sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Sonoma's inheritance: brambly, peppery, high-alcohol reds from head-trained old vines in Dry Creek Valley, Sonoma Valley and Alexander Valley, often field-blended with Petite Sirah and Carignan.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Napa's second red, the softening partner in proprietary blends and a plush varietal from Three Palms in Calistoga and the clay of Carneros.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Dry, sometimes oaked Fumé Blanc in Napa, grassy and crisp from Dry Creek Valley and Lake County, and the backbone of the valley's rare botrytised late-harvest wines.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Perfume and lift in Napa's Bordeaux blends, from Dominus to the Oakville cult wines, and occasionally a varietal from the mountains.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A dark seasoning in Napa's proprietary reds, ripening fully in the valley's heat.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Peppery, cool-climate Syrah from the Petaluma Gap and the Sonoma Coast, and riper versions from Sonoma Valley and Napa's hills.

grapes.name: Petite Sirah
grapes.styles: Durif, inky and tannic, the old field-blend partner of Zinfandel in Sonoma and Napa and a dark varietal on its own.

wines.note: Full-bodied and ripe: cassis, cedar, mocha and sweet oak, dusty tannin from the benches, firmer grip from the mountains. Decant the young ones; steak or lamb.
A Cabernet-led Bordeaux blend under a house name, Insignia 1974, Opus One 1979 and Dominus 1983 the models: polished, deep and long-lived.
Silky and perfumed: red cherry, cola and baking spice, soft tannin, fresh acid. Serve a touch cool with salmon or duck.
Brambly blackberry, black pepper and dried herbs at 14.5 per cent or more, from old head-trained vines with Petite Sirah and Carignan. Barbecue, ribs.
Traditional-method Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Carneros and Anderson Valley, Schramsberg's of 1965 the first: dry, toasty, the oyster wine.

made.viticulture: Vertical shoot positioning on cordon or cane is the rule, planted far denser than the old wide blocks since the AXR1 rootstock collapsed to phylloxera in the late 1980s and both counties replanted through the 1990s. Drip irrigation is normal, though the Rutherford bench and old Dry Creek Zinfandel are often dry-farmed, and old Zinfandel stays head-trained and hand-picked. Mountain vineyards above the fog line ripen in full sun on thin soils for small berries and firm tannin. Harvest runs from August for sparkling base to late October for mountain Cabernet, and the picking date, fresh acid against hang time, marks a house. The Agricultural Preserve of 1968 zoned Napa's floor for farming and is why the valley is not suburbs.
made.winemaking: Napa Cabernet is destemmed, cold-soaked, fermented warm with pump-overs, often given extended maceration, and matured eighteen to twenty-four months in largely new French oak; the top houses blend in Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot as proprietary reds. Silver Oak is the exception, in American oak alone. Chardonnay is barrel-fermented with lees stirring and some malolactic, though a leaner school, Stony Hill and Chateau Montelena its founders, keeps both down. Pinot Noir sees cold soaks, some whole bunches and 30 to 50 per cent new oak. Zinfandel ferments with its field-blend partners in older wood. Sparkling wine is traditional method: Schramsberg's 1965 Blanc de Blancs was America's first, Domaine Chandon followed in 1973 and Domaine Carneros in 1987.

law.classification: Everything here is an AVA or a county; no line carries a rule on grape, yield or style. North Coast is the 1983 umbrella over Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino, Lake, Marin and Solano. Napa Valley, California's first AVA in 1981, reached seventeen nested AVAs with Crystal Springs of Napa Valley in November 2024; Los Carneros and Howell Mountain were the first, in 1983. Sonoma County is a county appellation at 75 per cent with AVAs from Sonoma Valley to West Sonoma Coast of 2022; Los Carneros belongs to both counties. State law makes a Napa sub-AVA print Napa Valley, since 1990, and a Sonoma AVA print Sonoma County on wine bottled from 1 January 2014.
tiers: North Coast AVA
The 1983 umbrella over Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino, Lake, Marin and Solano counties; the origin on blends across the counties, from sparkling wine to Sauvignon Blanc.
Napa Valley AVA
California's first, 1981: most of the county, valley floor and hills, 85 per cent of the fruit from inside the line, and the name that must ride beside every nested AVA.
Nested Napa AVAs

Seventeen: Los Carneros, Howell Mountain, Wild Horse Valley, Stags Leap District, Mount Veeder, Atlas Peak, Spring Mountain District, Oakville, Rutherford, St Helena, Chiles Valley, Yountville, Diamond Mountain District, Oak Knoll District, Calistoga, Coombsville and Crystal Springs of Napa Valley.
Sonoma County
A county appellation, not an AVA: 75 per cent of the grapes from the county, and, on wine bottled from 1 January 2014, the name every Sonoma AVA label must also carry.
Sonoma AVAs

Sonoma Valley, Russian River Valley and its Green Valley, Chalk Hill, Dry Creek Valley and Rockpile, Alexander Valley, Knights Valley, Sonoma Coast with Fort Ross-Seaview and West Sonoma Coast, Petaluma Gap, Sonoma Mountain, Moon Mountain District, Bennett Valley, Fountaingrove District, Pine Mountain-Cloverdale Peak and Northern Sonoma.
Los Carneros AVA
The one AVA shared by both counties, 1983, open to San Pablo Bay: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base.
labels: Napa Valley beside a sub-AVA
Conjunctive labelling under California law since 1990: Oakville, Rutherford or Howell Mountain must print Napa Valley with it.
Sonoma County beside a Sonoma AVA
The same rule for Sonoma on wine bottled from 1 January 2014: Russian River Valley or Dry Creek Valley carries Sonoma County too.
Stags Leap District
The AVA, with no apostrophe; Stag's Leap Wine Cellars and Stags' Leap Winery are two houses inside it, spelt differently on purpose.
Rutherford dust
A tasting word for the fine, dusty tannin of Rutherford bench Cabernet, coined by the Russian-born winemaker who shaped Beaulieu from 1938; a style, not a soil or a rule.
To Kalon
The historic Oakville vineyard planted from 1868, long since divided among several owners, the Robert Mondavi Winery among them; a vineyard name, not an AVA.
Fumé Blanc
Dry Sauvignon Blanc under the name coined at Mondavi in 1968; no rule attaches to it.
Blanc de Blancs
A sparkling wine from white grapes only, in Napa and Carneros meaning Chardonnay; Schramsberg's of 1965 was the first in the country.

places.name: North Coast
places.note: The 1983 umbrella AVA over Napa, Sonoma, Mendocino, Lake, Marin and Solano counties, the origin on wines blended across them.

places.name: Mendocino County
places.note: Anderson Valley opens to the Pacific: cool Pinot Noir, Alsace whites and sparkling wine, Roederer's since 1982; Mendocino Ridge sits above about 366 metres (1,200 feet).

places.name: Lake County
places.note: Inland around Clear Lake on volcanic soils: Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet at elevation, Red Hills its best-known AVA.

places.name: Marin and Solano counties
places.note: The small ends: Marin's cold coastal Pinot Noir, Solano's Suisun Valley east of Napa.

places.name: Napa Valley
places.note: North of San Pablo Bay, cool south and hot north, where Cabernet Sauvignon took the gravelly benches and the valley's name; California's first AVA, 1981.

places.name: Los Carneros
places.note: The low southern hills shared with Sonoma, open to the bay's fog: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and the sparkling houses, 1983.

places.name: Coombsville
places.note: East of Napa city under the Vaca Range, cool and late, 2011: Cabernet of fresh acid on volcanic soils.

places.name: Oak Knoll District
places.note: The cool, foggy floor between Napa and Yountville, 2004: Merlot, Chardonnay and restrained Cabernet.

places.name: Yountville
places.note: The valley's first vines of the 1830s; Dominus farms Napanook here; supple, mid-weight Cabernet, 1999.

places.name: Stags Leap District
places.note: A pocket under the eastern palisades, 1989, argued from its soils: Cabernet of silk and perfume; Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, Shafer and Clos du Val.

places.name: Oakville
places.note: The prestige bench, 1993: To Kalon, Martha's Vineyard, Opus One, Harlan and Screaming Eagle; Cabernet of cassis, dust and power.

places.name: Rutherford
places.note: Next north on the same bench, 1993: the Rutherford dust Cabernet of Beaulieu, Inglenook, Caymus, Frog's Leap and Grgich Hills.

places.name: St Helena
places.note: The narrowing, sheltered valley around the town, 1995: Beringer, Charles Krug, Spottswoode, Corison and Joseph Phelps; ripe, plush Cabernet.

places.name: Calistoga
places.note: The hot northern end under Mount St Helena, approved late 2009, trimmed 2024: volcanic soils, Chateau Montelena, Eisele Vineyard, Three Palms, cool nights.

places.name: Crystal Springs of Napa Valley
places.note: The seventeenth nested AVA, in force from 15 November 2024, on the lower Vaca slopes between St Helena and Calistoga.

places.name: Mount Veeder
places.note: The Mayacamas above Carneros, 1990, the mountain AVA nearest the bay, cool and wet: tight, tannic Cabernet; Mayacamas Vineyards' 1889 winery.

places.name: Spring Mountain District
places.note: The Mayacamas above St Helena, 1993, steep and forested: structured Cabernet and Stony Hill's Chardonnay, made without new oak since 1952.

places.name: Diamond Mountain District
places.note: The Mayacamas above Calistoga, 2001, volcanic: Diamond Creek, founded 1968 for single-vineyard Cabernets, and Schramsberg's cellars of 1862.

places.name: Howell Mountain
places.note: The Vaca Range above about 427 metres (1,400 feet) and the fog, 1983: red volcanic soils, the grippiest, longest-lived Cabernet, Dunn its standard-bearer.

places.name: Atlas Peak
places.note: High in the Vaca Range east of Stags Leap, 1992: Cabernet and Sangiovese on volcanic soils.

places.name: Chiles Valley
places.note: A high, remote Vaca valley east of St Helena, 1999: late-ripening Zinfandel and Cabernet.

places.name: Wild Horse Valley
places.note: A small, windy AVA of 1988 on the ridge towards Solano, rarely on a label.

places.name: Pritchard Hill
places.note: Eastern hills above Lake Hennessey, a vineyard name, not an AVA: Chappellet since 1967, Colgin, cult Cabernets.

places.name: Sonoma County
places.note: West of the Mayacamas and more varied: fog for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, inland warmth for Cabernet and Zinfandel; the last mission, at Sonoma in 1823, brought the Mission grape to the county.

places.name: Sonoma Valley
places.note: Between the Mayacamas and Sonoma Mountain: Buena Vista of 1857, Gundlach Bundschu of 1858 and Hanzell of 1953; Zinfandel, Cabernet and Chardonnay.

places.name: Sonoma Mountain
places.note: Volcanic slopes west of Glen Ellen above the fog, 1985: Cabernet and Zinfandel with grip.

places.name: Moon Mountain District
places.note: The Mayacamas side, 2013, red volcanic soils: structured Cabernet and old Zinfandel at Monte Rosso.

places.name: Bennett Valley
places.note: A cool pocket south of Santa Rosa open to the Petaluma Gap, 2003: Merlot, Syrah and Chardonnay.

places.name: Russian River Valley
places.note: The fog-cooled plain west of Healdsburg, 1983, on Goldridge sandy loam: Sonoma's great Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Westside Road, Rochioli, Williams Selyem, Kistler.

places.name: Green Valley of Russian River Valley
places.note: The coolest corner around Sebastopol and Forestville, renamed in 2007: Iron Horse sparkling wine and taut Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chalk Hill
places.note: Volcanic ash and tuff north-east of Windsor, 1983, inside the Russian River Valley: rich Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Sonoma Coast
places.note: The vast 1987 AVA from the Pacific to the county's heart; the true coast above Fort Ross gives cold, saline Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah.

places.name: Fort Ross-Seaview
places.note: Ridgetop vineyards above the fog from about 280 metres (920 feet), 2012: intense, long-lived Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

places.name: West Sonoma Coast
places.note: The 2022 AVA that draws the line around the real coastal strip, Annapolis to Freestone.

places.name: Petaluma Gap
places.note: The wind gap from Bodega Bay inland, 2017, shared with Marin: thick-skinned Pinot Noir and Syrah of savoury depth.

places.name: Dry Creek Valley
places.note: The warm, gravelly valley north-west of Healdsburg, 1983: head-trained old Zinfandel, Ridge's Lytton Springs, grassy Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Rockpile
places.note: High ridges above Lake Sonoma from about 244 metres (800 feet), 2002: concentrated Zinfandel and Cabernet above the fog.

places.name: Alexander Valley
places.note: The warm upper Russian River, Healdsburg to Cloverdale, 1984, beyond most fog: rounder Cabernet, Jordan and Silver Oak's Alexander Valley bottling, Zinfandel on the benches.

places.name: Knights Valley
places.note: The warmest Sonoma AVA, 1983, between Alexander Valley and Calistoga: Cabernet and Chardonnay on volcanic and alluvial soils.

places.name: Northern Sonoma
places.note: A 1990 umbrella over the county's northern AVAs, made for one large house's estate wines.

places.name: Fountaingrove District
places.note: Volcanic hills north-east of Santa Rosa, 2015: Cabernet and Syrah between Chalk Hill and Sonoma Valley.

places.name: Pine Mountain-Cloverdale Peak
places.note: High ridges above Cloverdale at the county's northern tip, 2011, shared with Mendocino: Cabernet above the fog.

producers.name: Robert Mondavi Winery
producers.why: Oakville, 1966, the first large Napa winery built after Prohibition, the To Kalon vineyard, Fumé Blanc in 1968 and half of Opus One.

producers.name: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars
producers.why: Its 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon won the red flight of the 1976 Paris tasting; S.L.V., Fay and Cask 23 are its Stags Leap District wines.

producers.name: Chateau Montelena
producers.why: The Calistoga estate of 1882 whose 1973 Chardonnay won the white flight in Paris in 1976; its estate Cabernet is the other wine to know.

producers.name: Beaulieu Vineyard
producers.why: Rutherford, 1900, where the Georges de Latour Private Reserve, first made in 1936, set the Napa Cabernet model and the phrase Rutherford dust was born.

producers.name: Inglenook
producers.why: Founded at Rutherford in 1879 by a Finnish sea captain; Rubicon is its flagship Cabernet-based red and the estate was reunited under its historic name in 2011.

producers.name: Opus One
producers.why: The 1979 Oakville partnership of Napa's great promoter and a Bordeaux first growth: a Cabernet-led blend sold as a single proprietary wine.

producers.name: Dominus Estate
producers.why: Yountville's Napanook vineyard farmed in the Pomerol manner since the 1983 vintage; Bordeaux-minded, dry-farmed, savoury Cabernet with Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.

producers.name: Joseph Phelps Vineyards
producers.why: St Helena, 1973; Insignia of 1974 was Napa's first proprietary Bordeaux-style blend, and the house also planted the valley's first serious Syrah.

producers.name: Heitz Cellar
producers.why: The 1961 house whose Martha's Vineyard Cabernet from Oakville, first made in 1966, carries the famous eucalyptus and mint note.

producers.name: Harlan Estate
producers.why: The western hills of Oakville, first vintage 1990: the model of the Napa cult Cabernet, dense, profound and tightly allocated.

producers.name: Screaming Eagle
producers.why: Oakville, first vintage 1992, the scarcest and most expensive Napa Cabernet; Second Flight is its second wine.

producers.name: Caymus Vineyards
producers.why: Rutherford, 1972: Napa Cabernet in the plush, generous style, with Special Selection drawn from the best lots.

producers.name: Shafer Vineyards
producers.why: Stags Leap District; Hillside Select is its single-hillside Cabernet and One Point Five the estate blend named for a family's generation and a half.

producers.name: Duckhorn Vineyards
producers.why: St Helena, 1976, the house that made Napa Merlot serious, above all from the Three Palms vineyard in Calistoga.

producers.name: Silver Oak Cellars
producers.why: Founded 1972: Cabernet Sauvignon aged in American oak only, in two bottlings, Napa Valley and Alexander Valley.

producers.name: Frog's Leap
producers.why: Rutherford, 1981: dry-farmed, organically grown Cabernet, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc in a restrained style.

producers.name: Grgich Hills Estate
producers.why: Founded at Rutherford in 1977 by the winemaker of the Paris-winning Montelena Chardonnay; Chardonnay, Cabernet and a botrytised late-harvest wine.

producers.name: Cakebread Cellars
producers.why: Rutherford, 1973: a family house whose Napa Chardonnay and Cabernet are restaurant list staples across the country.

producers.name: Chappellet
producers.why: Pritchard Hill, 1967, among the first wineries on Napa's eastern hills; Mountain Cuvée is the entry blend and Signature the estate Cabernet.

producers.name: Kongsgaard
producers.why: Cult Napa Chardonnay from the Judge vineyard and the eastern hills, made slowly with long lees ageing, alongside Syrah and Cabernet.

producers.name: Paul Hobbs
producers.why: Sebastopol-based house making single-vineyard Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in the Russian River Valley and Cabernet from Coombsville and Oakville.

producers.name: Schramsberg Vineyards
producers.why: Jacob Schram's 1862 estate on Diamond Mountain, revived in 1965 to make the first American Blanc de Blancs by the traditional method; Mirabelle is its North Coast label.

producers.name: Beringer Vineyards
producers.why: St Helena, 1876, the valley's oldest continuously operating winery; Private Reserve Cabernet and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Charles Krug Winery
producers.why: Founded 1861, Napa's first commercial winery, and the house the Mondavi family bought in 1943 before the split that built the Oakville winery.

producers.name: Stony Hill Vineyard
producers.why: Spring Mountain, 1952: long-lived Chardonnay without new oak or malolactic, the valley's leanest classic.

producers.name: Mayacamas Vineyards
producers.why: The 1889 stone winery on Mount Veeder; austere, tannic mountain Cabernet, and a Paris 1976 entrant.

producers.name: Dunn Vineyards
producers.why: Howell Mountain, 1979: the standard for grippy, long-lived mountain Cabernet at modest alcohol.

producers.name: Diamond Creek Vineyards
producers.why: Diamond Mountain, 1968: Volcanic Hill, Red Rock Terrace and Gravelly Meadow, three single-vineyard Cabernets that taught Napa to bottle by soil.

producers.name: Spottswoode Estate
producers.why: An 1882 St Helena estate, winery from 1982, organically farmed since 1985; elegant Cabernet and Sauvignon Blanc.

producers.name: Corison Winery
producers.why: St Helena, 1987: Cabernet of balance and moderate alcohol from the benchland, with the Kronos vineyard's old vines.

producers.name: Clos Du Val
producers.why: Stags Leap District, 1972, French-founded; its 1972 Cabernet was a Paris 1976 entrant and won the ten-year rematch.

producers.name: Colgin Cellars
producers.why: Pritchard Hill cult Cabernet from the 1992 vintage, with the IX Estate and Tychson Hill wines.

producers.name: Eisele Vineyard Estate
producers.why: Calistoga's Eisele vineyard, planted to Cabernet in 1964, bottled under its own name since 2016 and biodynamically farmed.

producers.name: Hanzell Vineyards
producers.why: Sonoma Valley, 1953: credited with California's first French barriques and temperature-controlled stainless steel, and the model for serious Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: J. Rochioli Vineyards
producers.why: Westside Road in the Russian River Valley, Pinot Noir planted in 1968; the vineyard that fed Williams Selyem and made the valley's name.

producers.name: Williams Selyem
producers.why: From a garage in 1981 to the first cult Pinot Noir in California, from Rochioli and other Russian River Valley sites.

producers.name: Kistler Vineyards
producers.why: Founded 1979: single-vineyard Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the Russian River Valley and the Sonoma Coast in the Burgundian manner.

producers.name: Kosta Browne
producers.why: Sebastopol, 1997: rich, polished Pinot Noir from the Sonoma Coast and the Russian River Valley, among the most sought-after in the state.

producers.name: Littorai
producers.why: Founded 1993: biodynamically farmed, restrained Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from the Sonoma Coast and Anderson Valley.

producers.name: Marcassin
producers.why: A tiny Sonoma Coast estate whose Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the county's most allocated.

producers.name: Peter Michael Winery
producers.why: Knights Valley, 1982, an English-founded estate of French-named Chardonnays and Cabernets from the volcanic slopes of Mount St Helena.

producers.name: Chalk Hill
producers.why: The estate that gave the Chalk Hill AVA its fame: full Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc from the volcanic hills north-east of Windsor.

producers.name: Ravenswood
producers.why: Sonoma, 1976, the house that made old-vine Zinfandel a category under the slogan no wimpy wines.

producers.name: Buena Vista Winery
producers.why: Founded at Sonoma in 1857 by a Hungarian count, often called California's first premium winery and the start of the Sonoma story.

producers.name: Domaine Carneros
producers.why: The Carneros sparkling house Taittinger built in 1987, in a replica of its Champagne château; Le Rêve is its Blanc de Blancs.

producers.name: Domaine Chandon
producers.why: Moët's Yountville house of 1973, the first French Champagne investment in California and the start of the traditional-method wave.

producers.name: Iron Horse Vineyards
producers.why: Green Valley's sparkling estate since the late 1970s, poured at state dinners and the benchmark of Russian River bubbles.

producers.name: Jordan Vineyard
producers.why: Alexander Valley, 1972: Bordeaux-styled Cabernet and Chardonnay in a château built for the purpose, the valley's calling card.

producers.name: Seghesio Family Vineyards
producers.why: Healdsburg since 1895: Alexander and Dry Creek Zinfandel from old vines and Italian varieties.

exam: Draw Napa from south to north, Carneros to Calistoga, with the floor and bench AVAs in order and the mountain AVAs on the right side: Mayacamas west, Vaca east.
Say why the south is cool and the north hot, and why Sonoma's fog comes through the Petaluma Gap and up the Russian River.
Give the Paris pair, Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet and Chateau Montelena Chardonnay, both 1973, and the date 24 May 1976.
Match each Sonoma AVA to its grape: Russian River Valley Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Dry Creek Valley Zinfandel, Alexander Valley Cabernet, Sonoma Coast cold Pinot Noir.

Hold the dates that recur: Napa Valley 1981, Carneros and Howell Mountain 1983, Stags Leap District 1989, Oakville and Rutherford 1993, Petaluma Gap 2017, West Sonoma Coast 2022, Crystal Springs 2024.
Know the conjunctive labelling rules and that Sonoma County is a county at 75 per cent while Napa Valley is an AVA at 85.
At Advanced, know Goldridge soil, the AXR1 replanting, the three spellings of Stags Leap, To Kalon and Napanook, and the mountain AVAs' fog line.
Name the proprietary reds and their years: Insignia 1974, Opus One 1979, Dominus 1983, Harlan 1990, Screaming Eagle 1992.
traps: Napa and Sonoma are two counties with separate appellations; only Los Carneros is shared, and a Sonoma wine never says Napa.
Stags Leap District has no apostrophe; Stag's Leap Wine Cellars won Paris, and Stags' Leap Winery is a different house.
Chateau Montelena won with Chardonnay, not Cabernet, and Stag's Leap Wine Cellars with Cabernet, not Chardonnay.
Howell Mountain and Atlas Peak are in the Vaca Range on the east; Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain and Diamond Mountain are in the Mayacamas on the west.
Rutherford dust describes tannin texture, not a soil; the benches are gravelly alluvial fans, and the mountains are volcanic.
Sonoma Coast is a huge AVA that reaches far inland; the cold true coast is Fort Ross-Seaview and, since 2022, West Sonoma Coast.
Russian River Valley sits on Goldridge sandy loam, not on volcanic soil; Chalk Hill's ash and tuff is the volcanic corner of it.
Pritchard Hill and To Kalon are vineyard names that mean a great deal and no AVA at all.

cards.f: Napa's valley-floor and bench AVAs, south to north
cards.b: Los Carneros, Oak Knoll District, Yountville, Stags Leap District (east side), Oakville, Rutherford, St Helena, Calistoga; Coombsville sits east of Napa city and Crystal Springs below Howell Mountain.

cards.f: Napa's mountain AVAs: which range
cards.b: Mayacamas, west: Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain District, Diamond Mountain District. Vaca Range, east: Howell Mountain, Atlas Peak, Chiles Valley. Pritchard Hill in the east is a vineyard name, not an AVA.

cards.f: Why Carneros is cool and Calistoga hot
cards.b: Fog and wind enter from San Pablo Bay at the southern end and weaken as they travel north, so Carneros grows Pinot Noir and Chardonnay and Calistoga, about 50 kilometres north, ripens Cabernet in heat tempered by cool nights.

cards.f: Sonoma AVAs and their grapes
cards.b: Russian River Valley: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay. Sonoma Coast and Fort Ross-Seaview: cold Pinot Noir. Dry Creek Valley: Zinfandel. Alexander Valley: Cabernet. Knights Valley: warmest, Cabernet. Petaluma Gap: windy Pinot and Syrah.

cards.f: The three Stags Leap spellings
cards.b: Stags Leap District is the AVA, no apostrophe. Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, apostrophe before the s, won Paris 1976. Stags' Leap Winery, apostrophe after, is a separate house.

cards.f: Goldridge soil: where and why
cards.b: A fine sandy loam of old marine sediment under the Russian River Valley and Green Valley; free-draining and low in vigour, it gives the valley's Pinot Noir and Chardonnay their finesse.

cards.f: Napa proprietary reds and first vintages
cards.b: Insignia (Joseph Phelps) 1974, the first. Opus One (Mondavi with a Bordeaux first growth) 1979. Dominus (Napanook, Yountville) 1983. Harlan Estate 1990. Screaming Eagle 1992.

cards.f: Conjunctive labelling in the two counties
cards.b: Napa: a sub-AVA label must also print Napa Valley, state law of 1990. Sonoma: any AVA lying wholly in the county must also print Sonoma County, on wine bottled from 1 January 2014.

cards.f: Napa Valley's nested AVAs: how many by late 2024, and the last added
cards.b: Seventeen by November 2024. The first were Los Carneros and Howell Mountain in 1983; the seventeenth was Crystal Springs of Napa Valley, in force from 15 November 2024, on the Vaca slopes between St Helena and Calistoga.

cards.f: Los Carneros: what makes it unusual
cards.b: The only nested Napa Valley AVA that crosses into Sonoma County, approved in 1983 at the southern end, open to San Pablo Bay: cool, windy and foggy, for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base wine.

questions.q: Which nested Napa Valley AVA extends into Sonoma County?
questions.exp: Los Carneros straddles the county line at the southern end of both counties, open to San Pablo Bay; Oak Knoll, Yountville and Coombsville lie wholly in Napa.

questions.q: In which mountain range does Howell Mountain lie?
questions.exp: Howell Mountain rises on the Vaca side, east of St Helena; Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain and Diamond Mountain are the Mayacamas AVAs on the west, and the Santa Cruz Mountains and the Diablo Range lie well to the south.

questions.q: Goldridge sandy loam is the signature soil of which Sonoma AVA?
questions.exp: Goldridge, a fine, free-draining sandy loam of marine origin, underlies the Russian River Valley and gives its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay their finesse; Chalk Hill is its volcanic corner, and the benches of Dry Creek and Alexander valleys are gravel.

questions.q: Which house's 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon won the red flight of the 1976 Paris tasting?
questions.exp: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 from the Stags Leap District took first place; Heitz entered its 1970 Martha's Vineyard and placed lower, Chateau Montelena won the white flight with Chardonnay, and Trefethen did not compete.

questions.q: Which Sonoma AVA is known above all for old-vine Zinfandel?
questions.exp: Dry Creek Valley's warm, gravelly benches north-west of Healdsburg carry head-trained Zinfandel, some of it a century old; the other three are Pinot Noir country in the fog.

questions.q: Under California's conjunctive labelling law, which appellation must a Dry Creek Valley label also carry?
questions.exp: State law makes any AVA lying wholly in Sonoma County print Sonoma County beside it on wine bottled from 1 January 2014; Napa has required Napa Valley beside its sub-AVAs since 1990.

questions.q: Which historic Oakville vineyard, first planted in 1868, became the home of the Robert Mondavi Winery in 1966?
questions.exp: To Kalon was planted on the Oakville bench from 1868, and the Robert Mondavi Winery was built on part of it in 1966; like Heitz's Martha's Vineyard nearby, it is a vineyard name, not an AVA.

questions.q: Which Napa house ages its Cabernet Sauvignon in American oak only?
questions.exp: Silver Oak has aged its Cabernet Sauvignon in American oak alone since its founding in 1972, for both its Napa Valley and Alexander Valley bottlings, where new French oak is the Napa norm.

regions.name: Central Coast (CA)
regions.summary: The Central Coast is the Pacific strip from San Francisco Bay to Santa Barbara, an umbrella AVA of 1985 holding a set of climates; its rule is distance from the sea and whether the hills let the marine air in. The Santa Cruz Mountains make structured Cabernet above the fog; Monterey's Salinas Valley funnels wind to the Santa Lucia Highlands' Pinot Noir; Paso Robles, inland and hot by day, is Rhône and Zinfandel country on limestone; Santa Barbara's east to west valleys pour cold air onto the Pinot Noir and Chardonnay of Sta. Rita Hills.

terroir.climate: Maritime to Mediterranean by distance from the ocean. Wherever a valley opens to the cold California Current, Salinas, Santa Maria, Santa Ynez or the Templeton Gap, afternoon wind and morning fog hold temperatures down and stretch harvest into November. Sta. Rita Hills and the Santa Lucia Highlands are among the state's coolest sites; inland Paso Robles is hot by day, cold by night and dry.
terroir.soils: Marine sediment and uplift: calcareous shale and limestone on Paso Robles' west side, sandy marine deposits at Santa Maria and Sta. Rita Hills, Franciscan rock with limestone on Monte Bello Ridge, granite and limestone at Chalone and Mount Harlan in the Gavilan Range, gravel in Livermore, and deep sand at Oakley that kept phylloxera off century-old Zinfandel and Mourvèdre.
terroir.topography: Coast Ranges run north-west to south-east for most of the length: the Santa Cruz Mountains above the bay, the Gavilan and Santa Lucia ranges either side of the Salinas Valley. In Santa Barbara the ranges turn east to west and the valleys open onto the Pacific. Elevation defines the Santa Cruz Mountains AVA, 122 metres (400 feet) on the ocean side and 244 metres (800 feet) on the bay side.
terroir.water: The Pacific and Monterey Bay, with its deep submarine canyon, drive the climate; the Salinas River runs north to the bay, the Santa Maria and Santa Ynez rivers reach the sea, and Paso Robles draws scarce water from aquifers.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: The coastal grape of Santa Maria Valley, Sta. Rita Hills, the Santa Lucia Highlands, Mount Harlan and the Santa Cruz Mountains: from taut, red-fruited and spicy to dark, plush and savoury where the wind thickens the skins.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The most planted white grape of the Central Coast, from the big Salinas Valley crops to the serious cool-climate wines of Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Maria, Edna Valley and the Santa Cruz Mountains; the Wente clone that filled the state began in Livermore.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The Rhône Rangers' grape: peppery and cool from Santa Maria's Bien Nacido, Ballard Canyon and the Santa Lucia Highlands, dense and chocolatey from Paso Robles' west side.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted red of Paso Robles, ripe and generous; firm, mineral and long-lived from Monte Bello in the Santa Cruz Mountains and old-fashioned from Livermore; Happy Canyon ripens it at Santa Barbara's warm end.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Paso Robles' heritage red from dry-farmed head-trained vines, ripe and briary; old vines at Oakley in Contra Costa too.

grapes.name: Grenache
grapes.styles: The G of the Paso Robles and Santa Barbara GSM blends, perfumed and strawberry-scented, from cuttings the Tablas Creek nursery brought from the Rhône.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre
grapes.styles: Dark, meaty and structured in Paso Robles blends, and from century-old sand-grown vines at Oakley.

grapes.name: Viognier
grapes.styles: Apricot and honeysuckle in Paso Robles and Santa Barbara, varietal or co-fermented with Syrah; Roussanne and Marsanne are its Rhône companions here.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: A Rhône white of pear, honey and weight, in Paso Robles and Santa Barbara blends.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy and ripe from Happy Canyon and Santa Ynez Valley, and part of Livermore's old Sémillon blends.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Monterey's Arroyo Seco and Santa Barbara grow it dry and aromatic, and sometimes botrytised.

grapes.name: Chenin Blanc
grapes.styles: Chalone's old vines and a few Santa Barbara sites keep dry, nutty Chenin alive.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: A Chalone speciality from vines on limestone at about 550 metres (1,800 feet), nutty and full.

wines.note: Cool, perfumed and taut: cranberry, red cherry, dried herbs and a saline edge with bright acid. Lightly cool with duck or salmon.
Citrus, white peach and wet stone with creamy lees texture and fog-tunnel acid; Bien Nacido and the Sta. Rita Hills estates set the standard. Crab, chicken.
Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre in the Châteauneuf manner: blackberry, lavender, cocoa and warm spice at 14.5 per cent or more. Lamb, braises.
Monte Bello is the model: cassis, cedar, graphite and firm tannin from a cool limestone ridge, in American oak, built for decades.
From Bien Nacido or Ballard Canyon: black pepper, smoked meat, violets and blue fruit in a Northern Rhône register.

made.viticulture: Wind is the farmer. In the Salinas Valley and Sta. Rita Hills afternoon gales thicken skins, halt the vine each afternoon and stretch ripening into November, so rows often run with the wind; fog brings mildew and botrytis pressure, and autumn rain can beat the last Pinot Noir in. Paso Robles has the opposite problem: scant rain, days above 35 degrees, dry-farmed head-trained Zinfandel beside irrigated trellised blocks, and nights 20 degrees colder that keep the acid. The Rhône Rangers built on cuttings a Paso Robles nursery imported from Châteauneuf-du-Pape from 1989, so many of the Grenache, Mourvèdre and Roussanne vines planted since trace to one place. The Santa Cruz Mountains and Mount Harlan are farmed on thin limestone at elevation for tiny crops.
made.winemaking: Coastal Pinot Noir is made in the Burgundian manner: cold soak, some whole bunches, native yeasts and 20 to 50 per cent new French oak. Chardonnay is whole-bunch pressed and barrel-fermented on lees with partial malolactic, the Santa Barbara houses picking early for tension. The Rhône Rangers co-ferment Syrah with a little Viognier, blend Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre after separate fermentations and favour older wood, foudres and concrete over new barrels. Ridge at Monte Bello ferments with native yeasts, selects lots by tasting and ages in air-dried American oak. Paso Robles Cabernet and Zinfandel are made ripe and plush; Chalone and Calera keep the Burgundian methods their founders learnt in France.

law.classification: Central Coast is the umbrella AVA of 1985 from San Francisco Bay to Santa Barbara County; everything under it is a nested AVA or a county, none with a rule on grape, yield or style. San Francisco Bay, 1999, sits inside it over Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley and, since April 2024, Contra Costa. Santa Cruz Mountains, 1981, was the first AVA defined by elevation. The working units are the county and valley AVAs from Monterey to Santa Ynez Valley, which holds five nested AVAs. Paso Robles gained eleven districts in 2014, and state law has printed Paso Robles beside any of them since the 2008 bottling year.
tiers: Central Coast AVA
The 1985 umbrella from the bay to Santa Barbara County; the origin on blends across its counties and on much of the state's mid-priced Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
San Francisco Bay AVA
The 1999 AVA within the Central Coast over Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley and, since 15 April 2024, the Contra Costa AVA.
Santa Cruz Mountains AVA
1981, the first AVA defined by elevation: 122 metres (400 feet) on the ocean side and 244 metres (800 feet) on the bay side; Ben Lomond Mountain nests within it.
Monterey AVA
The county's 1984 AVA over the Salinas Valley; the county's smaller AVAs are Santa Lucia Highlands, Arroyo Seco, Chalone, Carmel Valley, San Bernabe, San Lucas, Hames Valley and San Antonio Valley.
Paso Robles AVA
1983, one of the largest AVAs in the state, with eleven districts approved in 2014 and conjunctive labelling under state law.
Santa Ynez Valley AVA
1983, with Sta. Rita Hills (2001), Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara (2009), Ballard Canyon (2013), Los Olivos District (2016) and Alisos Canyon (2020) nested inside it.
San Luis Obispo Coast AVA
2022, a coastal strip of San Luis Obispo County that takes in Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley; labelled SLO Coast.
labels: Paso Robles beside a district
Conjunctive labelling under California Business and Professions Code section 25244: a wine from any district of Paso Robles must print Paso Robles with it, for wine bottled from 1 January 2008.
Sta. Rita Hills
The AVA's legal spelling since 2006, abbreviated after a Chilean producer objected to Santa Rita; it is said in full as Santa Rita Hills.
Monte Bello
Ridge's estate Cabernet blend from Monte Bello Ridge in the Santa Cruz Mountains, a vineyard and brand name rather than an AVA.
Rhône Ranger
A nickname from the 1980s for the Central Coast houses that planted Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier and Roussanne; a movement, not a category.
Bien Nacido
A Santa Maria Valley vineyard planted in 1973 that many houses name on their labels; a vineyard designation, which under federal law needs 95 per cent from that vineyard.

places.name: San Francisco Bay
places.note: The 1999 AVA inside the Central Coast around the southern and eastern bay: Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley and Contra Costa.

places.name: Livermore Valley
places.note: East of the bay on gravel, 1982, Wente and Concannon since 1883: the Wente Chardonnay clone, Sémillon from Sauternes cuttings, Petite Sirah and Cabernet.

places.name: Contra Costa
places.note: An AVA from 15 April 2024 for the county's century-old, own-rooted Zinfandel, Mourvèdre and Carignan on sand at Oakley.

places.name: Santa Clara Valley
places.note: The old vineyards under Silicon Valley, largely built over, a few historic houses left.

places.name: Santa Cruz Mountains
places.note: The 1981 AVA defined by elevation between bay and ocean: Ridge's Monte Bello Cabernet on limestone between about 400 and 820 metres (1,300 and 2,700 feet) and Mount Eden's Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; Monte Bello 1971 was fifth in Paris, first in the 2006 rematch.

places.name: Monte Bello Ridge
places.note: Above Cupertino, where Ridge began in 1959; Monte Bello since 1962, in American oak; a vineyard, not an AVA.

places.name: Ben Lomond Mountain
places.note: A 1988 nested AVA on the ocean side above Santa Cruz, cold, forested and little planted.

places.name: Monterey
places.note: The county AVA of 1984 over the Salinas Valley, a wind tunnel from Monterey Bay: cool in the north for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, warm at King City for Cabernet.

places.name: Santa Lucia Highlands
places.note: Terraces above the Salinas Valley's west side, 1991, in fog and wind: dark, lush Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and cool Syrah.

places.name: Arroyo Seco
places.note: A gravelly river fan south of Soledad, 1983, wind-cooled: Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Chalone
places.note: Limestone and granite at about 550 metres (1,800 feet) in the Gavilan Range, 1982, vines from 1919: Chardonnay, Pinot Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Pinot Noir; a Paris 1976 entrant.

places.name: Carmel Valley
places.note: Behind Carmel in the Santa Lucias, 1983, sheltered and warmer: Cabernet and Merlot.

places.name: San Lucas and Hames Valley
places.note: The warm southern Salinas Valley around King City: Cabernet and Merlot on a large scale.

places.name: San Benito
places.note: Inland east of the Gavilan Range: Mount Harlan's limestone Pinot Noir, and the small Cienega Valley and Paicines AVAs on the San Andreas fault.

places.name: Mount Harlan
places.note: The 1990 AVA around Calera's limestone vineyards at about 670 metres (2,200 feet), planted from 1975 by a Burgundy-trained founder: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Viognier.

places.name: Cienega Valley
places.note: A 1982 AVA on the fault south of Hollister, old vines, with Lime Kiln Valley inside it.

places.name: San Luis Obispo County
places.note: Between Monterey and Santa Barbara: hot Paso Robles inland, cool Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley by the sea.

places.name: Paso Robles
places.note: The big inland AVA of 1983: hot days, cold nights, limestone on the hilly west, alluvium on the flat east; Cabernet most planted, old dry-farmed Zinfandel, Rhône blends at Tablas Creek and Saxum; eleven districts since 2014.

places.name: Adelaida District
places.note: Limestone hills of the north-west, high and cooled by the Templeton Gap: Tablas Creek, Rhône grapes, Cabernet, Zinfandel.

places.name: Willow Creek District
places.note: The calcareous west side south of Adelaida, among the coolest and wettest: Saxum's James Berry Vineyard and the Rhône cult wines.

places.name: Templeton Gap District
places.note: The gap in the Santa Lucias that admits the afternoon sea wind: Syrah, Zinfandel and Cabernet.

places.name: El Pomar District
places.note: Rolling hills south-east of Templeton, moderately cool: Rhône blends and Cabernet.

places.name: Paso Robles Estrella District
places.note: The broad warm plain along the Estrella River, widely planted: Cabernet and Merlot in volume.

places.name: Paso Robles Geneseo District
places.note: East of the town on the warm, dry floor: Cabernet, Zinfandel and Rhône reds.

places.name: Creston District
places.note: Higher ground south-east of the town, warm days and cold nights: Cabernet and Rhône grapes.

places.name: Paso Robles Highlands District
places.note: The far east at the highest elevations, hottest by day and coldest by night.

places.name: San Juan Creek
places.note: The hot, dry north-east corner with the lowest rainfall and few vineyards.

places.name: San Miguel District
places.note: The north around San Miguel's mission, warm and low: Cabernet and Zinfandel on alluvium.

places.name: Santa Margarita Ranch
places.note: The southern tip above the Cuesta Grade, cool and wet, a single historic ranch.

places.name: York Mountain
places.note: A tiny 1983 AVA west of Paso Robles in the Santa Lucias, cool and high.

places.name: Edna Valley
places.note: The cool valley south of San Luis Obispo open to Morro Bay's air, 1982: creamy citrus Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Rhône whites.

places.name: Arroyo Grande Valley
places.note: The next valley south, 1990, sea to inland: cool Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, old-vine Zinfandel inland.

places.name: San Luis Obispo Coast
places.note: The 2022 AVA along the shore, labelled SLO Coast, taking in Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley.

places.name: Santa Barbara County
places.note: Where the mountains run east to west and the valleys open to the Pacific: Pinot Noir at the cold western end, Cabernet at the warm eastern end; the film Sideways of 2004 was shot here.

places.name: Santa Maria Valley
places.note: The northern valley, 1981, open to the sea: fog, wind and sandy soils for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and cool Syrah; Bien Nacido of 1973, Au Bon Climat and Qupé since 1982.

places.name: Santa Ynez Valley
places.note: The southern valley, 1983, Lompoc east past Buellton and Solvang: cold at the sea, warm inland, five nested AVAs, Sanford & Benedict of 1971.

places.name: Sta. Rita Hills
places.note: The cold western end between Lompoc and Buellton, 2001, respelt in 2006: the state's most taut Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Sanford & Benedict, Sea Smoke, Sandhi.

places.name: Ballard Canyon
places.note: A north to south canyon in the valley's middle, 2013, largely Syrah and Rhône grapes with limestone pockets.

places.name: Los Olivos District
places.note: The warm, flat centre around Los Olivos, 2016: Rhône blends, Sauvignon Blanc and Sangiovese.

places.name: Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara
places.note: The hot eastern end beyond the fog, 2009: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Alisos Canyon
places.note: A 2020 AVA around Los Alamos between the two valleys: Rhône grapes in a moderate climate.

producers.name: Ridge Vineyards
producers.why: Founded 1959 on Monte Bello Ridge: Monte Bello Cabernet in American oak since 1962, fifth in Paris in 1976 and first in the 2006 rematch, and the old-vine Zinfandel blends of Lytton Springs and Geyserville in Sonoma.

producers.name: Mount Eden Vineyards
producers.why: A Santa Cruz Mountains estate on the vineyard a 1940s pioneer planted at about 610 metres (2,000 feet); Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet of Burgundian and Bordelais restraint.

producers.name: Bonny Doon Vineyard
producers.why: The Santa Cruz house of 1983 that led the Rhône Rangers with Le Cigare Volant, a Châteauneuf-style blend, and championed screwcaps and odd grapes.

producers.name: Calera Wine Company
producers.why: Mount Harlan, 1975: limestone-grown single-vineyard Pinot Noir, Jensen, Selleck, Reed and Mills, made in the Burgundian manner by a founder who had worked in the Côte d'Or.

producers.name: Chalone Vineyard
producers.why: The Gavilan Range estate on limestone at about 550 metres (1,800 feet), from vines of 1919; its 1974 Chardonnay was a Paris entrant and its Pinot Blanc and Chenin Blanc are unlike any other in the state.

producers.name: Tablas Creek Vineyard
producers.why: The 1989 Adelaida partnership of Château de Beaucastel's family and its American importer: the nursery that brought Rhône cuttings to America and the model Paso Robles GSM blends, Esprit de Tablas.

producers.name: Saxum Vineyards
producers.why: Willow Creek's James Berry Vineyard: the Paso Robles cult Rhône blends, dense and polished, tightly allocated.

producers.name: Turley Wine Cellars
producers.why: Templeton and St Helena: single-vineyard old-vine Zinfandel and Petite Sirah from Paso Robles, Napa, Sonoma, Amador and Lodi at full ripeness.

producers.name: Au Bon Climat
producers.why: Santa Maria Valley, 1982: the Burgundian Pinot Noir and Chardonnay that put Santa Barbara on the map, from Bien Nacido and the Sanford & Benedict vineyard.

producers.name: Qupé
producers.why: Founded 1982 beside Au Bon Climat at Bien Nacido: cool-climate Syrah, Marsanne and Roussanne in the Northern Rhône mould, a founding Rhône Ranger.

producers.name: Sanford Winery
producers.why: The house of the Sanford & Benedict vineyard, planted in 1971, which proved Pinot Noir could ripen in the Sta. Rita Hills' wind.

producers.name: Sandhi
producers.why: Sta. Rita Hills Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of restraint, early picking and neutral oak, from a Lompoc cellar at the centre of the modern lean-Chardonnay movement.

producers.name: Gainey Vineyard
producers.why: A Santa Ynez Valley family estate of 1984 with vineyards in the Sta. Rita Hills, pouring cool-climate Chardonnay and Pinot Noir by the glass across the country.

producers.name: Piedrasassi
producers.why: A Lompoc cellar making savoury, peppery Syrah from Bien Nacido and other Santa Barbara sites in the Northern Rhône style.

producers.name: Sine Qua Non
producers.why: Ventura County's cult Rhône-style house, from 1994, with vineyards in Santa Barbara County; every wine carries a new name and label, and the allocations are among the most sought in America.

producers.name: Wente Vineyards
producers.why: Livermore since 1883, the oldest continuously family-owned winery in the state, and the source of the Wente Chardonnay clone that planted California.

producers.name: Concannon Vineyard
producers.why: Livermore since 1883, credited with the first varietally labelled Petite Sirah in the 1960s and with Cabernet clones used across the state.

producers.name: Talley Vineyards
producers.why: Arroyo Grande Valley's family estate from 1986: cool Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the Rincon and Rosemary vineyards.

producers.name: Alban Vineyards
producers.why: Edna Valley, 1989, the first American estate given wholly to Rhône grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Viognier and Roussanne of cult standing.

producers.name: Justin Vineyards
producers.why: Paso Robles' west side since 1981; Isosceles, a Bordeaux blend, gave the district its first national reputation for Cabernet.

producers.name: Brewer-Clifton
producers.why: Sta. Rita Hills from 1996: whole-cluster Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from single vineyards, among the first to show the AVA's style.

producers.name: Sea Smoke
producers.why: A Sta. Rita Hills estate on the south-facing bluffs above the Santa Ynez River, from 1999: plush, dark Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Foxen Vineyard
producers.why: Santa Maria Valley's Foxen Canyon house of 1985, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Rhône wines from Bien Nacido and its own vineyards.

producers.name: Talbott Vineyards
producers.why: The Sleepy Hollow vineyard in the Santa Lucia Highlands, planted in 1972, and the Chardonnay that made the AVA's name.

exam: Say the governing rule: distance from the ocean and the gaps in the hills decide the climate, more than latitude.
Explain Santa Barbara's transverse ranges, and why Sta. Rita Hills in the west grows Pinot Noir while Happy Canyon in the east grows Cabernet.
Place Paso Robles inland with limestone on its west side, hot days, cold nights, Rhône grapes, Zinfandel and the most Cabernet; Tablas Creek is the Rhône nursery.
Know Ridge Monte Bello: Santa Cruz Mountains, Cabernet-led, American oak, fifth in Paris 1976 and first in the 2006 rematch.
Match Monterey's wind to the Santa Lucia Highlands and its Pinot Noir, Chalone to limestone and Pinot Blanc, and Mount Harlan to Calera.
Name Bien Nacido, Sanford & Benedict and Monte Bello as the vineyards, and Au Bon Climat, Qupé and Bonny Doon as the Rhône Rangers' houses.
Hold the dates: Santa Maria Valley 1981, Santa Cruz Mountains 1981, Paso Robles 1983, Central Coast 1985, Sta. Rita Hills 2001, the Paso districts 2014, SLO Coast 2022, Contra Costa 2024.
traps: Central Coast is not the Central Valley: the coast is Pacific fog and Pinot Noir, the valley is the hot interior of bulk wine.
Santa Barbara's valleys run east to west, so the western end is the cold one; in Napa and the Salinas Valley the cold end is the one nearest the bay.
Sta. Rita Hills is spelt with the abbreviation by law since 2006 and lies inside the Santa Ynez Valley, not beside it.
Paso Robles is in San Luis Obispo County, not Santa Barbara; Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande are its cool coastal neighbours in the same county.
Ridge Monte Bello is Cabernet from the Santa Cruz Mountains in American oak; Ridge's Zinfandels, Lytton Springs and Geyserville, are Sonoma wines.
Chalone is in Monterey County and Mount Harlan is in San Benito, on opposite sides of the same Gavilan Range.
The Santa Lucia Highlands are terraces above the Salinas Valley floor, not the valley itself, and the Santa Lucia Range also walls Paso Robles from the sea.
Bien Nacido and Sanford & Benedict are vineyards, not AVAs; a vineyard designation needs 95 per cent from that site.

cards.f: The Central Coast's governing rule
cards.b: Distance from the Pacific and the gaps in the Coast Ranges decide the climate more than latitude: Sta. Rita Hills, well south of Paso Robles, is far cooler because its valley opens straight to the sea.

cards.f: Santa Barbara's transverse ranges: why they matter
cards.b: The Santa Ynez and San Rafael mountains run east to west, so the valleys open onto the Pacific: Sta. Rita Hills in the cold west grows Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Happy Canyon in the warm east grows Cabernet.

cards.f: Paso Robles in one line
cards.b: Inland San Luis Obispo County, 1983: hot days, cold nights, calcareous shale and limestone on the west, alluvium on the east; Cabernet most planted, old Zinfandel, Rhône blends; eleven districts since 2014; Tablas Creek the Rhône nursery.

cards.f: Ridge Monte Bello: place, grape, oak, Paris
cards.b: Monte Bello Ridge, Santa Cruz Mountains, limestone from about 400 to 820 metres; Cabernet-led Bordeaux blend; American oak; first vintage 1962; fifth in Paris 1976, first at the 2006 thirtieth-anniversary rematch.

cards.f: What cools the Santa Lucia Highlands, and what grows there
cards.b: Monterey Bay's cold water sends an afternoon wind down the Salinas Valley; the Santa Lucia Highlands, terraces on its west wall, 1991, grow dark, lush Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and cool Syrah.

cards.f: The Santa Ynez Valley's five nested AVAs
cards.b: Sta. Rita Hills (2001, west, Pinot and Chardonnay), Ballard Canyon (2013, Syrah), Los Olivos District (2016, centre), Happy Canyon of Santa Barbara (2009, east, Cabernet), Alisos Canyon (2020, Rhône grapes).

cards.f: Three vineyards every Central Coast list names
cards.b: Bien Nacido (Santa Maria Valley, 1973: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah). Sanford & Benedict (Sta. Rita Hills, 1971: the area's first Pinot Noir). Monte Bello (Santa Cruz Mountains, Ridge's Cabernet).

cards.f: The Rhône Rangers: who and what
cards.b: Central Coast houses of the 1980s that planted Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier and Roussanne: Bonny Doon's Le Cigare Volant, Qupé's Syrah, Alban in Edna Valley, Tablas Creek's nursery from Beaucastel in Paso Robles.

cards.f: Limestone Pinot Noir in the Gavilan Range: the two AVAs
cards.b: Chalone (Monterey side, about 550 metres, vines from 1919, also Pinot Blanc and Chenin Blanc) and Mount Harlan (San Benito side, Calera, 1975, single-vineyard Pinot Noir and Viognier).

cards.f: Conjunctive labelling for Paso Robles
cards.b: Business and Professions Code section 25244: a wine from any Paso Robles district must print Paso Robles beside the district's name, for wine bottled from 1 January 2008; the eleven districts arrived in 2014.

questions.q: Which was the first California AVA to have its boundary drawn by elevation?
questions.exp: The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA of 1981 follows the 122-metre (400-foot) contour on its ocean side and 244 metres (800 feet) on its bay side; Howell Mountain's 427-metre (1,400-foot) line came in 1983, Mount Harlan in 1990 and the Santa Lucia Highlands in 1991.

questions.q: Which AVA occupies the western end of the Santa Ynez Valley?
questions.exp: Sta. Rita Hills takes the cold western end between Lompoc and Buellton, nearest the Pacific, for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; Ballard Canyon and Los Olivos District lie in the middle and Happy Canyon at the warm eastern end.

questions.q: Which Paso Robles estate was founded in 1989 as a partnership with the family of Château de Beaucastel?
questions.exp: Tablas Creek in the Adelaida District imported Rhône cuttings from Beaucastel, ran them through quarantine and sold them on, which is why so many Grenache, Mourvèdre and Roussanne vines across the state trace to it.

questions.q: Which San Luis Obispo County AVA lies inland of the Santa Lucia Range, with hot days and cold nights?
questions.exp: Paso Robles, behind the Santa Lucia Range, swings from hot days to cold nights; Edna Valley and Arroyo Grande Valley are the county's cool coastal valleys, and York Mountain is a tiny, cool AVA in the hills to its west.

questions.q: Which Santa Maria Valley vineyard, planted in 1973, appears on labels from Au Bon Climat, Qupé and many other houses?
questions.exp: Bien Nacido is the valley's most named vineyard, sold to many houses for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah; a vineyard designation needs 95 per cent from that site under federal law.

questions.q: How many district AVAs were approved inside Paso Robles in 2014?
questions.exp: Paso Robles was divided into eleven districts in 2014, from Adelaida and Willow Creek on the limestone west to Estrella and Geneseo on the warm eastern floor; As of 2026 Napa Valley holds seventeen nested AVAs and the Santa Ynez Valley five.

questions.q: On which kind of soil does Calera grow its Pinot Noir on Mount Harlan?
questions.exp: Calera's founder searched California for limestone after working in Burgundy and found it at about 670 metres (2,200 feet) in the Gavilan Range; Goldridge is the Russian River Valley's soil, red volcanic soil Howell Mountain's, and granite lies beside limestone at Chalone.

questions.q: Which Ridge wine led the reds at the 2006 rematch of the 1976 Paris tasting?
questions.exp: The 1971 Monte Bello, a Cabernet-led blend from the Santa Cruz Mountains, placed fifth in 1976 and first among the reds at the thirtieth-anniversary retasting in 2006, when the Californian wines outlasted the Bordeaux.
